qs.q: Approximately what percentage of infected women are estimated to have no symptoms at all when infected with Chlamydia trachomatis?
qs.e: Chlamydia is known as a silent disease because about 70% of infected women and 50% of infected men experience no symptoms at all. The other figures listed do not correspond to the asymptomatic rate in women.

qs.q: Which diagnostic test is considered the most sensitive method available for detecting Chlamydia trachomatis genetic material?
qs.e: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) find the DNA of Chlamydia bacteria and are the most sensitive tests available with minimal risk of false negatives. Cell culture and EIA are either less sensitive, more expensive, or slower.

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman is evaluated for contact with a partner recently diagnosed with a Chlamydia trachomatis infection. What is the typical incubation period for this bacterial pathogen?
qs.e: The incubation period for Chlamydia trachomatis is typically between 7 and 21 days. An interval of 1 to 2 days is far too short and is instead characteristic of acute bacterial gonococcal infections.

qs.q: Ophthalmia neonatorum is a form of neonatal conjunctivitis that can be acquired during birth from mothers infected with Chlamydia trachomatis and which other pathogen?
qs.e: Ophthalmia neonatorum is caused by vertical transmission of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis during passage through an infected birth canal. Both agents can cause severe conjunctivitis and potential corneal blindness if left untreated.

qs.q: A child presents with pink eye disease (trachoma/infection) linked to Chlamydia trachomatis. Which mechanical vector is noted for carrying this agent?
qs.e: Musca species (flies) transmit Chlamydia trachomatis causing pink eye disease. Blatta orientalis transmits Vibrio cholerae.
qs.s: Medical Entomology: High-Yield Tables and Key Facts: MCQs

qs.q: A group of subjects is found to have Chlamydia trachomatis infection. Which of the following laboratory methods is most likely to be useful in diagnosis of C. trachomatis?
o: Cytologic smear preparation of the affected tissue
Enzyme immunoassay detection of specific antigens
Darkfield microscopic examination of exudate or secretions
Histological analysis of a tissue biopsy specimen
qs.e: This is the easiest and most cost-effective method, since C. trachomatis cannot be easily cultured by routine methods.

qs.q: Ophthalmia neonatorum, a severe conjunctivitis, is associated with Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, which are sexually transmitted infections.
o: Treponema pallidum and Herpes simplex virus
Human immunodeficiency virus and Hepatitis B virus
qs.e: Ophthalmia neonatorum is a serious eye infection in newborns. The most common causes are Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, both of which are sexually transmitted infections acquired during passage through the birth canal.

qs.q: Salpingitis, inflammation of the fallopian tubes, is most commonly caused by sexually transmitted infections like Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Syphilis is not a primary cause of salpingitis and does not typically lead to gumma formation in the fallopian tubes.
o: Gonorrhea and Chlamydia; pelvic inflammatory disease
qs.e: Salpingitis is a key component of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID). The most common causative agents of PID and salpingitis are Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Syphilis does not typically cause salpingitis or gumma formation in the fallopian tubes.
